worgle-answer-today.articleHtml:

Welsh uses letters in ways that trip up English-trained solvers. Today's answer contains a doubled consonant that signals Welsh orthography rather than English morphology. How to read common Welsh digraphs without overforcing them

Welsh has several two-letter combinations that count as single sounds. DD makes the voiced TH as in "that." FF produces an F sound, not a double-eff. NG works like English but appears more frequently in Welsh words because of grammatical endings. LL is a voiceless alveolar lateral fricative—there is no equivalent in standard English, so most solvers skip it entirely until forced. These digraphs sit in the middle of words more often than English speakers expect, which means green tiles can land in unexpected positions if you treat each letter individually.

The letter Y functions as either a vowel or a consonant depending on position. At the start of words it usually acts like an English Y. In the middle or end, it often replaces I or U sounds. This dual nature explains why Y appears roughly three times more often in Welsh Wordle solutions than in English ones. A careful player checks whether Y is acting as a vowel before committing a guess.

Where English guessing habits break the solve

English Wordle players develop instincts around Q followed by U, words ending in S, and the rarity of X and Z in final positions. Welsh throws these patterns out. Words can end in letters that feel impossible to English ears. The absence of Q in standard Welsh vocabulary means one common English opening move becomes useless here. Players who started with AUDIO or QUEEN on today's board wasted both guesses on invalid letter combinations.

Double letters appear more freely in Welsh orthography. What looks like an improbable pattern on the board—two identical consonants separated by one other letter—may actually be a legitimate Welsh word. The trick is treating each tile as provisional until you've confirmed the letter pool matches Welsh vocabulary rather than assuming English rules apply.

Some players try to force familiar English roots into Welsh patterns. This rarely works. Welsh etymology diverged from English centuries ago, so looking for cognates leads to dead ends. The better strategy treats Welsh as its own system and builds guesses from Welsh letter-frequency data instead.

If Worldle places your guess northeast of center and at roughly 40% of the true distance, you know two things simultaneously: the target country sits in that cardinal quadrant, and it's not a neighbor—it's geographically removed from your guess by a meaningful margin.

The percentage isn't arbitrary. It maps to real kilometers scaled to the globe, so a 12% result means your guess and the answer occupy different hemispheres more often than not. Players who treat the distance figure as flavor text miss the constraint it provides. Combine direction and distance before your next guess, not after.

But Worldle rewards geographic precision over regional intuition. A country sharing a border with the target will almost always score above 60% distance similarity, which means you're still far off even when the shape seems familiar.

Does the distance percentage correspond to real kilometers?

Yes. Worldle calculates the shortest great-circle distance between your guessed capital city and the target's capital, then expresses it as a percentage of Earth's total circumference. A lower number means the capitals are closer together geographically.
